expectations.text: Identifies that during the rollout window old code runs against the new schema
expectations.evidence: For the minutes between the migration running and the last old pod draining, old code is still `SELECT`ing `legacy_email` against a schema that no longer has it — every request on those paths 500s.

expectations.text: Recommends splitting into separate deploys (expand/contract) rather than shipping the drop with the code
expectations.evidence: Deploy A (today, Friday, fine): the code-only removal of the three reads. Deploy B (Monday/Tuesday morning): the `DROP`, alone.

expectations.text: States that dropping the column is irreversible without a backup or restore
expectations.evidence: The `DROP COLUMN`. Nothing restores it. Not a revert, not a redeploy — the data is gone the instant the migration runs.

expectations.text: Addresses what rollback looks like if the deploy goes wrong
expectations.evidence: Worse: your rollback is now the broken artifact. Reverting the deploy reintroduces code that reads a dropped column.

expectations.text: Addresses the Friday timing in terms of who is available to respond, not as superstition
expectations.evidence: Friday isn't superstition — it's staffing... it shouldn't land when the people who'd do a restore are heading out.

expectations.text: Recommends a CI gate that blocks destructive DDL from landing alongside application code
expectations.evidence: A CI check that fails any PR containing `DROP COLUMN`/`DROP TABLE`/`TRUNCATE` in a migration *alongside* application code changes.

expectations.text: Does not approve the merge as-is on the strength of green CI
expectations.evidence: Deploy A reverts in minutes, so ship it. Deploy B has no rollback at any speed, which is exactly why it shouldn't land.

expectations.text: Distinguishes the reversible parts of the change from the irreversible part
expectations.evidence: This PR is one reversible change and one irreversible change stapled together... Deploy A... Deploy B.
